Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

vignette: Kanaq Tiare sat quietly in his living room, surrounded by the remnants of a life once shared with his late wife. As an interior designer, he had always taken pride in creating warm and inviting spaces for others, but now his own home felt empty and cold. It had been two years since his captivity ordeal, during which he was held hostage by militants who spoke only Arabic. The memory of those days still lingered, often resurfacing unexpectedly like a slap to the face. The sound of shouting in Arabic could send Kanaq's mind racing back to that cramped, dingy room where he was held captive. He would relive the helplessness and fear as his captors yelled at him, demanding answers he didn't have. Even now, when he heard similar sounds - perhaps a TV show or a conversation between strangers - Kanaq's body would tense up before his mind even registered what was happening. His heart racing, he'd feel an overwhelming urge to flee, to escape the confines of the space and find safety. To cope with these triggers, Kanaq had developed a habit of rehearsing conversations before any social interaction. He'd script out potential questions and responses in his head, trying to anticipate every possible scenario. This exhausting mental exercise left him feeling drained but also slightly more prepared for the uncertain world outside. At work, however, this coping mechanism often fell short. The thought of entering enclosed spaces - like meeting rooms or client homes - made Kanaq's skin crawl. He'd avoid work-related events or appointments whenever possible, citing vague excuses to his colleagues. Despite his best efforts, feelings of vulnerability and anxiety still lingered, making everyday tasks feel daunting. When he did venture out, Kanaq found himself constantly scanning the room for potential threats, positioning himself with his back against a wall so he could see everything around him. This hyper-vigilance left him exhausted but also eerily calm - as if his body had taken over to compensate for his fragile emotional state. When trying to explain what happened during those fateful days in captivity, Kanaq's words would falter and fail him. He'd struggle to articulate the events leading up to his capture or the conditions he faced while held prisoner. Emotionless recall took hold, making it feel as though someone else had experienced the ordeal - a stranger whose memories Kanaq was merely borrowing. Sometimes, in the stillness of night, Kanaq would hear the muffled sounds of Arabic chanting or yelling in his head, transporting him back to that dingy room. He'd wake up with a start, drenched in sweat and clinging to his pillow as if it were a lifeline. As he lay there, trying to calm himself down, Kanaq couldn't shake off the feeling that something was watching him from the shadows - waiting for its chance to pounce. It was this constant sense of unease that finally drove Kanaq to seek help. The weight of his memories and emotions had become too much to bear alone. As he navigated the dark waters of his trauma, Kanaq held onto a glimmer of hope: perhaps, with the right guidance, he could learn to tame these inner demons and rediscover some semblance of peace in his life.
